claims.summary: Randomized encryption without an enclave lacks server-side equality search. It is a legitimate choice when the application only stores and retrieves ciphertext without that search requirement, not for this parameterized lookup.

Deterministic Always Encrypted supports equality comparisons on this supported bigint column, with the stated encrypting driver and external keys. It preserves the required client/engine boundary but still reveals equality patterns.
TDE encrypts files, logs and backups at rest while the engine still processes plaintext during authorized queries. It fits a storage-theft requirement, not the specified separation from the engine.
DDM limits returned presentation for readers lacking UNMASK and leaves stored data unchanged. It is useful for accidental display exposure, not keeping plaintext outside the engine.

sourceReviews.supportingSummary: Inspected Configure Always Encrypted, Limitations and Database permissions in the MCP body. Deterministic encryption permits equality point lookups; randomized encryption without enclaves cannot search encrypted columns. The driver encrypts parameters, plaintext keys remain outside the engine, and deterministic ciphertext discloses equality patterns. bigint avoids the documented string-collation requirement; literal comparisons are not substituted for the stipulated parameters.

The actual training text distinguishes file-at-rest TDE from client-side Always Encrypted and explicit server-side column encryption. Its encryption-layer paragraph directly references the cited Always Encrypted article. I use its TDE distinction, not its unqualified suggestion that no Always Encrypted configuration ever processes plaintext in an enclave.

Overview, Permissions and the security note establish that DDM changes query results, not stored values, and is not a cryptographic barrier to the database engine. It is a useful presentation control but cannot satisfy the client-versus-engine encryption requirement.

choiceReviews.rationale: The Always Encrypted article explicitly excludes searching randomized ciphertext without secure enclaves. Randomized encryption is a real choice for stronger pattern concealment when these server-side lookups are unnecessary, or with separately configured supported enclave operations; neither context is this stem.

The documented deterministic mode supports equality point lookups while an enabled client driver encrypts parameters and decrypts results outside the engine. The bigint column, parameterization and external-key access remove the principal type, literal and client prerequisites relevant to this selection. Equality-pattern leakage remains possible.

The encryption unit assigns TDE to files, logs and backups at rest and explicitly says it does not protect against appropriately authorized database users. TDE can preserve normal querying while protecting stolen storage, but that is not exclusion of plaintext from normal engine processing.

The masking article says underlying data is unchanged and masking is applied to query results. DDM fits limiting accidental display exposure to restricted readers; it neither encrypts the bigint values for the engine nor implements the required external-key boundary.

review.verificationNotes: Independently derive B, not a general endorsement of every Always Encrypted deployment. SQL Server 2022 and the no-enclave boundary are explicit; the sources document the applicable released SQL features, not an unknown-maturity methodology. No executable snippet is present; the parameter and type conditions were inspected. The negative-wording warning is necessary to exclude enclave behavior, and 'Always' is a feature name rather than an absolute secrecy promise. Advanced is defensible as a two-constraint protection/query tradeoff: randomized encryption meets the trust boundary but not the lookup, whereas TDE preserves lookup behavior but not that trust boundary. This is the preserved dp800-direct-013 lineage, not a new duplicate; its fact differs from the symmetric-key session prerequisite in d2-001. PASS 2 only.
review.confidenceReason: High confidence in the uniquely supported key from the actual encryption and masking bodies, with the deterministic-pattern limitation retained. This review is source-based, not a claim to have executed an Always Encrypted client.

optionChallenges.couldBeCorrectWhen: Randomized encryption is appropriate when protected columns need no server-side searching, grouping or joins. Enclave-enabled confidential comparisons are a different architecture explicitly excluded here.
optionChallenges.evidenceSummary: The Always Encrypted article expressly excludes searching randomized encrypted columns without secure enclaves. Randomized encryption still protects the client/engine boundary, but cannot satisfy the required server-side parameterized equality lookup. It fits storage/retrieval without such predicates, or a separately designed enclave-enabled solution; neither is the stated workload.

optionChallenges.claimRepresented: Deterministic Always Encrypted without an enclave supports the encrypted equality lookup while plaintext keys and values stay outside the ordinary engine.
optionChallenges.whyIncorrectInContext: Supported, not incorrect: the article's deterministic equality exception and client-parameter contract match the requested operation and trust boundary.
optionChallenges.couldBeCorrectWhen: The application uses a supported encrypted type, matching encryption metadata and an enabled driver with key access, and accepts equality-pattern leakage. It would not solve an unmentioned range-search requirement.
optionChallenges.evidenceSummary: Configure Always Encrypted permits deterministic point lookups, and Limitations requires client-encrypted parameters instead of plaintext literals. Those prerequisites and external-key access are supplied. This is supported, not incorrect: deterministic encryption meets both stated constraints without enclaves, although repeated ciphertext can disclose equality patterns.

optionChallenges.claimRepresented: TDE alone prevents the database engine from handling plaintext during the lookup.
optionChallenges.whyIncorrectInContext: Storage encryption does not provide the stipulated runtime separation between the application and database engine.
optionChallenges.couldBeCorrectWhen: TDE is suitable when the requirement is protection of files and backups at rest with ordinary server-side queries, or as a complementary layer rather than the sole control.
optionChallenges.evidenceSummary: The encryption unit identifies TDE as protection for database files, logs and backups at rest and explicitly says it does not protect data from authorized connected users. TDE alone leaves normal engine plaintext processing available. It can protect stolen storage or complement Always Encrypted, but does not meet this client-only plaintext requirement.

optionChallenges.claimRepresented: Dynamic Data Masking alone supplies the same cryptographic engine boundary as client-side encryption.
optionChallenges.whyIncorrectInContext: Masking governs returned presentation, not where encryption keys or plaintext values are processed.
optionChallenges.couldBeCorrectWhen: Masking is an additional exposure-reduction control for authorized readers of predefined queries; it is not a substitute when administrators or the engine must not see plaintext.
optionChallenges.evidenceSummary: The DDM article says stored values are unchanged and masking is applied to query results for restricted readers. Its inference warning further rejects treating masking as full protection from ad hoc queries. DDM alone can reduce accidental display exposure, but is not encryption and cannot keep the engine from processing plaintext.

claims.summary: SELECT enables reading every column but does not itself unmask Phone. Combined with the narrowly scoped Phone UNMASK grant, it supplies precisely the separate access and presentation permissions required.
Table UNMASK would reveal both masked columns once SELECT is granted. That is suitable for a role authorized to see all masked columns on Contact, but too broad for Phone-only disclosure.
SQL Server 2022 supports column-scoped UNMASK. Phone-column UNMASK together with SELECT reveals Phone while leaving Email masked under the explicitly closed permission baseline.
ALTER ANY MASK governs mask administration, with table ALTER additionally required to change definitions. It fits a mask-maintenance task, not reading data with unchanged mask definitions.

sourceReviews.supportingSummary: Inspected Permissions, SQL Server 2022 granular permissions and the column/table UNMASK examples. SELECT supplies table reads; UNMASK is separately scopeable down to a column starting in SQL Server 2022. Table UNMASK is broader, and changing a mask requires ALTER ANY MASK plus table ALTER. The source also excludes a claim of inference-proof secrecy.

choiceReviews.rationale: Permissions states that SELECT on a table permits reading its data; UNMASK by itself does not grant reads. With the stem's closed effective-permission baseline, table SELECT is necessary to read every column while the existing masks remain.

The granular examples distinguish table UNMASK from column UNMASK. At table scope it exposes both Phone and Email once SELECT is granted. It is appropriate when both masked columns may be revealed, not the stipulated Phone-only presentation.

The SQL Server 2022 section expressly permits column-scoped UNMASK and demonstrates GRANT UNMASK ON table(column). Applying that scope to Phone, together with table SELECT, changes Phone presentation without unmasking Email under the explicitly closed permission baseline.

ALTER ANY MASK is for adding, replacing or removing mask definitions, also requiring ALTER on the table. It is useful for a mask-administration role, not a read/unmask grant, and changing definitions is expressly outside this task.

review.verificationNotes: Independently derive the complete two-selection set A,C. The question correctly pins SQL Server 2022 rather than implying granular UNMASK on all historical versions. Its exclusion of inherited grants, DENYs and administrative access is important because CONTROL implies unmasking. Grant descriptions are technically valid; no executable code is claimed tested. Intermediate implementation difficulty fits combining read permission with a narrower presentation permission. The preserved ID is a refresh of its own baseline, not a new item; d2-002 instead concerns values physically copied by a masked reader. No grammar, length or answer-count ambiguity found. PASS 2 only.
review.confidenceReason: High confidence: the product article directly states both permissions, the 2022 scope enhancement and the mask-administration prerequisites; all four choices can be distinguished without assuming hidden grants.

With the necessary SELECT, this would expose both Phone and Email, contrary to the Phone-only exception. Table UNMASK is appropriate for a reader approved to see all masked columns in that table.

optionChallenges.evidenceSummary: The granular-permissions section and column UNMASK example explicitly support a column-scoped exception beginning with SQL Server 2022. Phone-column UNMASK paired with table SELECT is supported, not incorrect: it reveals Phone while leaving Email masked under the stipulated absence of overriding grants, DENYs, CONTROL or module access.

optionChallenges.evidenceSummary: Permissions describes ALTER ANY MASK as mask-definition administration, with table ALTER additionally required to add, replace or remove a mask. It supplies neither the SELECT nor UNMASK grant requested here, and changing the mask is explicitly prohibited. It fits an authorized mask-maintenance task instead.

claims.summary: A FILTER predicate controls access to stored rows for SELECT, UPDATE and DELETE. It can hide a newly inserted row from later reads, but does not reject that INSERT merely because the row would be hidden.
BEFORE UPDATE evaluates the old rows targeted for update. It can block changes to already-disallowed rows, not validate the new values of an INSERT.
BEFORE DELETE protects removal of existing rows. It is the appropriate timing for a deletion restriction and is not invoked as the INSERT new-value gate.
AFTER INSERT block predicates reject inserted values that violate the enabled policy. The platform is explicitly SQL Server 2022, avoiding unsupported cross-platform block-predicate assumptions.

sourceReviews.supportingSummary: Inspected Description, predicate behavior and Permissions. Filter predicates govern visible/readable existing rows; INSERT can create rows later filtered from reads. AFTER INSERT block predicates check the inserted values and fail violating writes. BEFORE UPDATE and BEFORE DELETE are separate operation-specific checks. SQL Server is supported; Fabric/Synapse block-predicate parity is not inferred.

choiceReviews.rationale: The source explicitly allows INSERT of a row that a filter will hide during later operations. A FILTER predicate is appropriate for limiting visible existing rows, but does not by itself reject these newly inserted values.

BEFORE UPDATE applies to existing rows targeted for an update. It can prohibit updating a row that currently violates the condition, but INSERT is a different operation with a different predicate event.
BEFORE DELETE can block deletion of existing rows, which is a valid RLS write restriction. It is not fired as the inserted-row check required by this INSERT question.

The article identifies AFTER INSERT as a block-predicate event evaluating the newly inserted row and says violating block operations fail with an error. This is the exact operation and resulting-state check requested.

review.verificationNotes: D is uniquely correct. The stem is mechanism selection, not a complete CREATE SECURITY POLICY script; an operative predicate/policy is implicit in choosing the mechanism, and no unmentioned principal exemption is needed. SQL Server 2022 supports the released RLS behavior first introduced in SQL Server 2016. Beginner/concept-recall is honest for this operation/timing distinction. Before/after alternatives have genuine uses rather than invented features. Preserved baseline lineage is retained, and the policy schema-binding permission diagnosis in d2-003 tests a different fact. PASS 2 only.
review.confidenceReason: High confidence because the RLS product article separately states filter INSERT behavior and all three block-event alternatives; no claim depends on unsupported Fabric write predicates.

optionChallenges.claimRepresented: A filter predicate alone rejects creation of a row because its new values fail the visibility predicate.
optionChallenges.whyIncorrectInContext: The documentation explicitly allows inserting a row that a later filter would hide; visibility filtering is not the requested write rejection.
optionChallenges.couldBeCorrectWhen: Use a filter to restrict readable rows or rows eligible for UPDATE/DELETE, with a separate block predicate if new values must also be prohibited.
optionChallenges.evidenceSummary: The RLS description says filter predicates affect SELECT, UPDATE and DELETE visibility and still allow inserting rows that will subsequently be filtered. A filter alone therefore does not reject this INSERT. It is appropriate for hiding existing rows from reads or preventing selection of rows to update/delete.

optionChallenges.claimRepresented: A BEFORE UPDATE block predicate checks new values in an INSERT operation.
optionChallenges.whyIncorrectInContext: The selected event is UPDATE rather than INSERT, and its timing addresses existing rather than newly inserted state.
optionChallenges.couldBeCorrectWhen: It can reject updates to rows whose current values fail a policy; that is a different operation/state pair from this question.
optionChallenges.evidenceSummary: BEFORE UPDATE checks whether existing rows targeted by an update currently violate the predicate. It is not triggered as the after-insertion validation of newly created row values. It is appropriate when an update must be blocked based on the row's pre-update state.

optionChallenges.claimRepresented: A BEFORE DELETE block predicate supplies INSERT-time validation.
optionChallenges.whyIncorrectInContext: Deleting existing rows is not the insertion operation whose new values must be rejected.
optionChallenges.couldBeCorrectWhen: A policy that must prevent removing protected rows can use BEFORE DELETE; its legitimate purpose does not make it an INSERT control.
optionChallenges.evidenceSummary: The RLS description assigns BEFORE DELETE to blocking deletion of existing rows. It does not validate newly inserted values. It is a legitimate block predicate when deletion itself is the prohibited write operation.

optionChallenges.claimRepresented: An AFTER INSERT block predicate rejects inserted values that violate the security predicate.
optionChallenges.whyIncorrectInContext: Supported, not incorrect: the documented operation and timing directly match new-row write validation.
optionChallenges.couldBeCorrectWhen: An enabled SQL Server security policy binds the block predicate to the insertion target. Do not transpose the answer to Fabric/Synapse products where the cited article excludes block support.
optionChallenges.evidenceSummary: Description lists AFTER INSERT as a block operation and states that a violating block predicate makes the write fail with an error. This is supported, not incorrect, because the question requires checking newly inserted row values. It assumes a correctly bound, enabled policy; merely declaring an unused or disabled predicate would not enforce anything.

claims.summary: TDE protects files at rest and can be useful alongside column encryption. It does not open the existing symmetric key needed by this ENCRYPTBYKEY operation.
An Always Encrypted driver supports client-side column encryption with external keys. This operation deliberately uses server-side ENCRYPTBYKEY and an existing database key instead.

The linked column-encryption examples open the certificate-protected symmetric key before ENCRYPTBYKEY and DECRYPTBYKEY. That supplies the missing step without changing the specified encryption design.
A mask changes returned presentation and can reduce accidental display exposure. It neither opens AccountKey nor performs the specified cryptographic operation.

sourceReviews.supportingSummary: Inspected security prerequisites and both encryption examples. A certificate protects an AES symmetric key, a varbinary column stores ciphertext, and OPEN SYMMETRIC KEY ... DECRYPTION BY CERTIFICATE precedes ENCRYPTBYKEY(KEY_GUID(...), column). The simple example does not require an authenticator argument. This is server-side column encryption, not client-side Always Encrypted.

The training's column-encryption section independently demonstrates opening the certificate-protected key before ENCRYPTBYKEY, then closing it. Its layer comparison assigns TDE to storage and Always Encrypted to a client/engine trust separation, distinguishing the otherwise real alternative controls.

The actual DDM overview says query-result masking does not alter stored values. It supports rejecting a mask as a substitute for opening a cryptographic key, while preserving masking's legitimate display-limiting use.

choiceReviews.rationale: TDE is a real at-rest protection for files and backups, and may coexist with column encryption. Nothing in its documented layer role opens AccountKey for this ENCRYPTBYKEY session; the explicit symmetric-key prerequisite remains unmet.

An Always Encrypted-enabled driver serves client-side encryption using its own key metadata and external key access. The displayed statement instead uses a database symmetric key through ENCRYPTBYKEY; enabling that driver is not the documented OPEN SYMMETRIC KEY step.

Both the product's simple symmetric example and the training place OPEN SYMMETRIC KEY ... DECRYPTION BY CERTIFICATE before ENCRYPTBYKEY. AccountKey exists but is closed, and the protecting certificate is usable in the authorized session, so this is the missing operation.

A mask changes returned presentation for masked readers and does not operate the symmetric key. It is suitable for display exposure reduction, but cannot perform the cryptographic setup required by the shown update.

review.verificationNotes: C is supported. Statically inspected the UPDATE, ENCRYPTBYKEY and KEY_GUID call shape against the actual simple-encryption example. nvarchar(20) plaintext and varbinary(256) destination do not introduce a plausible size/type conflict; existing key/certificate and authorized maintenance conditions avoid repeating creation prerequisites. No SQL execution was performed or runtime error invented. The mandatory wording is specific to this closed key, not every encryption method; 'this session' has a clear referent. Intermediate operational prerequisite selection is appropriate. Distinct from direct-013's client/engine boundary and deterministic lookup choice. PASS 2 only.
review.confidenceReason: High confidence from two inspected encryption bodies and a separately checked masking contrast; source examples directly establish the necessary key-opening order.

claims.summary: The product article says SELECT INTO by a reader without UNMASK writes masked values to the target. Those stored zeroes are not hidden originals, so an authorized re-extraction is needed if real values are legitimately required.
Source UNMASK would let that reader see originals in a fresh authorized source query. It does not retroactively change values already materialized in a different table.
Removing a mask can reveal underlying values when that table actually has a mask over real stored data. Here the copy has no mask definition and its stored data is already the masked output.
Partial masking exposes portions of stored string values; it does not recover information lost during an export and is not the numeric default-mask recovery mechanism.

sourceReviews.supportingSummary: Inspected the default-mask table, Permissions, export/copy behavior and mask removal examples. A numeric default mask returns zero; SELECT INTO by a reader without UNMASK materializes masked data in the destination. Ordinary masking leaves the source unchanged, and changing permission or dropping a mask exposes underlying data only where that data still exists.

choiceReviews.rationale: The documented SELECT INTO/export rule places masked values into the new table. Given that this destination physically holds zeroes and has no mask, its missing originals must come from a new authorized source extraction, not from a presentation-permission change on the copy.

UNMASK with SELECT permits a fresh query to retrieve unmasked source values. The article distinguishes that presentation rule from masked values already materialized in another table; rereading that existing copy does not rerun the extraction or restore lost information.

DROP MASKED is valid for removing a real mask from a column that still stores original data. This question expressly states the copy has no mask definition and stores zeroes, so mask removal cannot reveal originals there.

The product table describes partial masking as a custom string display function, not recovery of numeric values. Even on an eligible string column it can expose only portions of that column's stored value; it cannot reconstruct data lost in the earlier masked copy.

claims.summary: AVG gives each statistics row equal weight and yields 505 here. It measures the mean of interval means, which could be intended with equal interval weighting, but not the mean per execution.

The teaching query weights each duration average by count_executions and divides by the summed counts. Here total duration is 2,000 over 101 positive-count executions, so this expression uses the required denominator.
The weighted sum reconstructs total duration, 2,000, and would answer a total-resource-use question. Without division by 101 it does not compute the requested per-execution mean.
MAX returns 1,000, the largest supplied interval average. It is useful for identifying the largest aggregate interval mean, not the mean across all executions or a maximum individual execution.

sourceReviews.supportingSummary: Query the Query Store with T-SQL explicitly sums avg_duration multiplied by count_executions and divides by total executions, with NULLIF and rounding in its broader example. Runtime statistics are aggregates per interval. This supports weighting the supplied complete, positive-count rows, not a claim that a last_execution_time filter perfectly trims a real time window.

choiceReviews.rationale: The ordinary average of 10 and 1000 is 505: the row with one execution receives the same weight as the row with 100. AVG(avg_duration) would suit an intentionally equal-weight average of row means, or coincidentally equal execution counts, neither of which is the requested per-execution mean.

The observed training query uses execution-count weighting. Independently, total duration is 10*100 + 1000*1 = 2000 and the count is 101, giving approximately 19.801980198. The float duration in the supplied derived table prevents integer division, and the positive complete inputs make the denominator nonzero.

The numerator reconstructs represented total duration, 2000, but has not normalized by 101 executions. It would answer a total-duration question, not the requested mean. The unit's weighted-mean expression includes the missing denominator explicitly.

MAX(avg_duration) returns 1000, the larger aggregate row mean. It can rank the worst interval mean, not the combined per-execution mean; it also must not be described as the maximum individual execution duration.

review.verificationNotes: Independent answer: b. claims.summary: Retrying only the failed statement would omit the first UPDATE because the entire victim transaction was rolled back. A statement-only retry can be meaningful for a different operation whose unit of work is that single statement.
COMMIT finalizes a surviving transaction; error 1205 has already rolled back this victim transaction. It cannot preserve the original transaction's first update.
Waiting for a lock can resume an ordinarily blocked transaction before victim selection. Once 1205 is returned, the old transaction does not survive to resume.

A fresh transaction must repeat both updates after the safe bounded delay. The explicit absence of external effects and safe whole-operation retry premise are essential; arbitrary business operations are not automatically retryable.

sourceReviews.supportingSummary: Deadlock detection and Handle deadlocks state that error 1205 follows rollback of the victim transaction; all its work is undone. Handle with TRY...CATCH permits catching the error, and retry guidance recommends a brief randomized pause. Ordinary blocking instead waits on a surviving transaction.

choiceReviews.rationale: The victim is the entire explicit transaction, not just its second UPDATE. Retrying only that statement loses the rolled-back first UPDATE and no longer repeats the stated atomic operation. A one-statement unit of work would be a different case.

Error 1205 reports rollback of the original victim transaction, so its changes cannot be committed afterward. A CATCH block can still run, but that control-flow continuation does not mean the original transaction survived.

Waiting may allow an ordinarily blocked, still-live transaction to resume after its blocker completes. Here victim selection and error 1205 have already ended the original transaction. A delay is useful before a new attempt, not to resume the rolled-back attempt.

Starting a new transaction and repeating both UPDATEs reconstructs the complete atomic operation after rollback. The bounded retry, randomized pause and absence of external effects satisfy the recovery assumptions; this does not license unbounded retries or repeating a non-idempotent external action.

review.verificationNotes: Independent answer: d. The actual product guide supports SQL Server 2022's mature 1205/transaction rollback behavior and catching the error; no Preview or edition-specific mechanism is invoked. Victim-selection priorities are irrelevant because selection already occurred; I did not adopt the training unit's oversimplified cheapest-victim rule. No executable retry snippet is authored here, and no SQL was executed. Approval does not endorse an unconditional second ROLLBACK of an already rolled-back transaction. The module summary directly links the exact Deadlocks guide, with complete course/path ancestry inspected. Intermediate troubleshooting is appropriate for interpreting a two-statement atomic boundary. Its longer correct option expresses that boundary without persuasive qualifiers. The baseline/live record has this same canonical ID and fact; the separate SNAPSHOT candidate adds stale read-derived calculation semantics, and the sleeping-blocker candidate has no victim/error-1205 event. PASS 2 only.
review.confidenceReason: High confidence from the product guide's explicit transaction-wide rollback and randomized retry guidance. Safe whole-operation retry and absence of external effects are supplied, so neither statement-only recovery nor survival of the old transaction remains defensible.

optionChallenges.claimRepresented: Recovery can repeat only the failing second UPDATE while preserving the first UPDATE’s contribution.
optionChallenges.whyIncorrectInContext: Victim rollback removed both statements’ work. Replaying the second alone constructs a different operation and omits the first update.
optionChallenges.couldBeCorrectWhen: If one autocommit statement is the complete safely retryable transaction, repeating that statement repeats the complete unit. The actual example contrasts an autocommit UPDATE with a multi-statement explicit transaction.
optionChallenges.evidenceSummary: Handle deadlocks identifies transaction rollback, and the demonstration labels Session A’s explicit transaction and Session B’s autocommit statement. That sourced boundary, not which statement errors, decides retry scope.

optionChallenges.claimRepresented: The original victim transaction remains available to commit after error 1205.
optionChallenges.whyIncorrectInContext: The engine has already rolled it back. Catching the error provides control flow, not a committable original transaction.
optionChallenges.couldBeCorrectWhen: COMMIT finalizes a live, committable transaction whose work completed without victim rollback. In the source’s same-order example, the first transaction commits or rolls back before the blocked transaction continues.
optionChallenges.evidenceSummary: Deadlock detection and Handle deadlocks describe rollback before 1205 is returned. Access objects in the same order separately describes normal commit, supporting the legitimate non-victim context.

optionChallenges.claimRepresented: Waiting for the conflicting lock to disappear lets the original victim transaction continue.
optionChallenges.whyIncorrectInContext: That describes a still-blocked request. The stipulated 1205 event has terminated this transaction, and waiting cannot restore its rolled-back state.
optionChallenges.couldBeCorrectWhen: Under ordinary non-deadlocked blocking, before victim termination or another abort, the requester can proceed when the owner releases its lock.
optionChallenges.evidenceSummary: Understand deadlocks explicitly contrasts normal lock waiting with monitor-selected victim termination. The recovery section recommends a brief wait before resubmission, not continuation of the discarded transaction.

claims.summary: RCSI selects a committed view per statement. It suits statements that may observe fresh commits between reads; it does not give this multi-statement report one transaction-level view.

SERIALIZABLE uses locking to protect reads and ranges, which conflicts with freely committing overlapping ordinary updates. It is appropriate when that blocking is acceptable to enforce serializable access.

SNAPSHOT uses a transaction-level committed versioned view once data access establishes the transaction snapshot. The read-only, no-DDL/no-hint conditions exclude writer conflicts and schema-lock cases that would need separate analysis.
READ UNCOMMITTED permits dirty reads and supplies no stable committed transaction snapshot. It can suit explicitly approximate reads that tolerate those anomalies, not this consistent report.

sourceReviews.supportingSummary: Reread Lock-based isolation levels and Row-versioning isolation levels: READ UNCOMMITTED permits dirty observations, SERIALIZABLE protects read ranges, RCSI reads a statement snapshot, and SNAPSHOT supplies a consistent view across statements. The enabling database option and explicit session selection are documented; universal no-blocking language is not accepted.

The actual product text dates row-versioned READ COMMITTED and SNAPSHOT to SQL Server 2005, distinguishes their version-selection boundaries and places the XSN at first data access. SERIALIZABLE retains data/range locks; versioned reads still acquire Sch-S and can encounter Sch-M contention. These sections independently bound the repaired question.

choiceReviews.rationale: Consider a commit after the first SELECT and before the next. RCSI can use that newer committed version for the next statement even inside the same explicit transaction. That is useful when each statement should see fresh committed data, but it cannot guarantee this report's common transaction-wide view.

SERIALIZABLE can keep the read set consistent by retaining shared and applicable range locks, but that prevents conflicting updates from freely committing and does not provide the requested versioned read view. It would fit a requirement that accepts this locking to enforce serialization, not both conditions in the stem.

With ALLOW_SNAPSHOT_ISOLATION enabled and the session using SNAPSHOT, successive reads use the transaction's version-selection boundary rather than resampling at each statement. Ordinary row writers are not blocked by shared data-read locks. First data access establishes the snapshot; schema-lock and update-conflict exceptions are not being denied.

READ UNCOMMITTED can observe an uncommitted writer's value that is later rolled back, as well as changing values across reads. Avoiding shared read locks does not make those observations a stable committed snapshot. Only a task explicitly tolerating such inconsistency could use that trade-off.

claims.summary: A SNAPSHOT update detects a row changed by a transaction that committed after its snapshot and terminates on conflict. Application-managed retry must use a new snapshot and reevaluate the decision rather than retaining a stale computed balance.
Waiting can resolve ordinary lock blocking while a transaction is still valid. Here the other writer has committed and the snapshot transaction has encountered a terminating update conflict.

A new transaction could accept an update based on a fresh valid context, but reusing the old calculation skips the business decision against the now-current balance. It does not preserve the stated read-calculate-write consistency.
A successful uncontested SNAPSHOT write can commit normally. An update conflict instead terminates the transaction; it is not evidence that the intended debit was accepted.

sourceReviews.supportingSummary: Reread Modify data without optimized locking: a SNAPSHOT update detects an intervening committed row modification and terminates the conflicting transaction. Applications must handle and retry those conflicts, including the noted constraint/indexed-view cases. The optimized-locking section preserves this SNAPSHOT rule rather than granting RCSI's automatic retry behavior.

The SNAPSHOT discussion confirms stable reads do not authorize silently overwriting a competing write. A business operation that reads, calculates and writes depends on the read value; the isolation setting does not independently validate a calculation reused after a conflict. The unit's flawed overselling illustration is not treated as a proof.

choiceReviews.rationale: The conflict invalidates the old transaction. Repeating the complete read-calculate-write operation in a new snapshot rechecks the debit against the changed balance instead of transporting a stale result. The absence of external effects and permission for bounded retries make this a valid recovery strategy, not a guarantee every retry will succeed.

The other writer has already committed, and the first transaction encountered a terminating snapshot conflict. There is no still-valid failed transaction to resume merely by waiting. Waiting would address an active lock owner before ordinary blocking ends; it cannot undo this abort or validate the old computed value.

Opening a new transaction does not refresh the balance used in the old absolute UPDATE result. Such a value could erase the effect of the concurrent transaction, for example an intervening credit. A newly validated conditional/idempotent operation would require a different contract; this option explicitly skips the necessary reread.

Conflict detection reports that this write attempt cannot complete under its snapshot; it is not a successful concurrency-validation result. A transaction whose update validation succeeds can commit, but the described terminated attempt has no accepted original debit to commit.

claims.summary: The pre/post product article separates calculation from execution, and the compare-project article generates deployment SQL from the current target. Completing a prerequisite before that generation makes its resulting schema an input. The testing unit supports validating the full sequence on a dedicated target, not assuming ordering proves safety.

PreDeploy is a real supported deployment hook, but the source explicitly places plan calculation before it executes. This workflow is useful for compatible preparation before plan execution; it does not change the target schema used in that already completed calculation.
PostDeploy is a real supported hook that runs after the deployment plan completes. It can handle post-schema work, but cannot supply a prerequisite schema state needed when that plan is calculated.

Generating and reviewing a saved deployment script is supported. That artifact represents the target state used at generation, however; performing a separate prerequisite afterward does not automatically regenerate it. The workflow can suit compatible intervening preparation, not a requirement to calculate from the new schema.

sourceReviews.supportingSummary: Reread the opening product contract and project-item examples. The deployment plan is calculated before PreDeploy executes; PreDeploy then precedes plan execution, and PostDeploy follows completion. These are actual stage boundaries, not filename rules. The article also excludes pre/post scripts from object-model validation, so correct ordering alone is not implementation-safety proof.

Reread Deploy report and Review deployment T-SQL scripts in the actual frozen article. Plan/report generation compares the source model with the connected target, and Script materializes the target-specific T-SQL for later review and execution. A prerequisite completed before this generation can change the input schema; executing a previously generated file does not itself request a fresh comparison.

Reread the testing-level and integration sections. Structural builds do not establish runtime correctness; multi-operation integration tests use a deployed dedicated database and known state. This supports the explanation's requirement to validate the prerequisite and full sequence on the isolated target, not a guarantee that the selected ordering makes any migration safe.

choiceReviews.rationale: Completing the prerequisite first means the later source-to-target comparison reads its resulting schema. Generating, reviewing and executing the script afterward therefore meets the specific planning-input requirement. The proposed order remains subject to the explanation's separate validation of actual schema and data effects.

A supported PreDeploy hook executes before the schema plan runs, but only after that plan has been calculated. Including it in the generated combined script does not execute its prerequisite while the comparison is reading the target. This workflow can perform preparation compatible with an already calculated plan, not supply the required new comparison state.

The documented PostDeploy hook executes after the schema plan, so it is later still than plan calculation. It is suitable for tasks such as populating objects after their creation, but cannot make a prerequisite schema mutation visible to the calculation that generated that same plan.

The saved script is generated and reviewed before the prerequisite changes the target. Running the prerequisite before executing the saved file changes execution conditions but does not regenerate that file from a new comparison. A previously approved script may remain valid after compatible preparation; that possibility does not meet this explicit requirement to calculate from the changed schema.

B and C are genuine pre/post mechanisms with wrong timing for this requirement; D is a genuine saved-script process but has already captured the old planning input. The prior final-context concerns are addressed: the stem no longer announces a false assumption or stale-plan diagnosis, all four options include review, and their lengths are 103/101/102/110 characters. The learner must distinguish calculation from execution rather than choose the only cautious workflow. Intermediate now matches this single sequencing decision; architecture-design is a broad workflow category, not an Advanced claim. Permissions and the isolated target are explicit. No rename/refactor implementation, automatic replan, rollback, atomicity or universal migration-safety guarantee is inferred. GA is bounded to the documented SQL-project hooks and SqlPackage script-generation contract, without a preview graphical-tool claim. There is no executable candidate code and no live build, comparison or deployment was run; codeReviewed records static stage semantics. The pronoun warning resolves to the changed target schema and saved script. This is distinct from direct-017's action/output selection and direct-018's reference-row convergence; no scoped duplicate was found. All original and earlier repair review records are preserved.

claims.summary: A model build validates syntax and references. It is useful for structural changes but does not establish the invoice amount or end-to-end inventory effects.
The testing unit distinguishes Scalar Value from Row Count. A deterministic expected total tests the calculation rather than merely the existence of one row.
Row Count is appropriate when cardinality is the requirement. The supplied defect preserves row count while changing the amount, so this does not address it.

Integration tests exercise sequences across procedures, triggers and tables. An isolated, known-state database lets this test observe cross-object effects that a single-value unit test does not cover.

The captured build section checks model references and target-platform syntax, then emits the dacpac. It supplies structural validation, not execution of invoice arithmetic or inventory transitions. I exclude its overly broad repeat-deployment-idempotence statement from this candidate's evidence.

choiceReviews.rationale: The already-green model build has not executed either business operation. Repeating that structural gate cannot reveal the wrong scalar or inconsistent end state; it remains useful for syntax/reference defects, a different class of failure.
For a deterministic fixture, a Scalar Value condition compares the invoice-total cell to its expected amount. This detects the stated defect even though the result still contains exactly one row.

Substituting another cardinality check for value checking cannot distinguish two one-row results containing different amounts. A Row Count condition is legitimate when quantity is the contract, but is insufficient for this specified scalar-value defect.

Executing the related procedures and trigger in a deployed isolated database, then asserting order and inventory state, exercises the cross-object workflow that the training assigns to integration testing. This addresses the second risk rather than duplicating the scalar test.

claims.summary: The CDC article says that when transactional replication is present, its log reader serves both replication and CDC capture. Restoring that shared process addresses the observed dependency while keeping both features.
A dedicated capture job is typical when CDC runs without transactional publications. The source explicitly describes its absence when the replication log reader performs capture instead.

Reinitialization can be appropriate for an intentionally replaced capture configuration, but it is not the documented coexistence repair. The replication log reader is intentionally shared, and recreating capture can disrupt the retained consumer contract.

Checkpoint can participate in normal log management, but the article says CDC-marked changes must be captured before their log truncation boundary advances. It cannot replace the stopped shared capture process.

sourceReviews.supportingSummary: The SQL Server/Managed Instance CDC article's Relationship with log reader agent section states that transactional replication's reader serves both replication and CDC when both are enabled. Agent jobs explains why a separate capture job is absent with transactional publications. The article also says pending capture prevents log truncation and CHECKPOINT cannot substitute for capture. This is not Azure SQL Database's separate scheduler contract.

choiceReviews.rationale: In the stated coexistence configuration, the replication Log Reader Agent invokes the shared log-reading path for replication and CDC. Resolving its stoppage restores that documented dependency without removing either consumer.

Agent jobs explicitly makes a dedicated CDC capture job conditional on there being no transactional publication. Its absence is expected here and cannot prove CDC was never enabled, especially given prior capture progress.

The source describes automatic switching between the standalone capture job and shared transactional reader as replication status changes. Recreating CDC while retaining the publication does not turn the documented shared architecture into a second independent capture path.

The article explicitly states that CHECKPOINT cannot truncate still-uncaptured CDC-marked changes when capture is stopped. A checkpoint does not read and publish the pending changes for either consumer.

review.verificationNotes: Derived a from the source's two operating modes, not merely from a generic CDC-is-asynchronous statement. SQL Server 2022, an existing transactional publication, prior successful CDC progress and a running SQL Server Agent distinguish the stopped replication reader from a stopped service or unconfigured capture. GA applies to this established SQL Server coexistence behavior; Azure-hosted consumer location does not change the source database platform. No job was started, CDC reset performed or CHECKPOINT executed. Advanced is defensible for recognizing intentional capture-job absence and shared replication/CDC internals while preserving both consumers, though the third reviewer should still score difficulty independently. The absolute warning concerns a disproved 'never enabled' inference, not an approved universal claim. Compared with archived 063-066: latency, captured-column transitions, operation codes and retention-window failures require different reasoning.
review.confidenceReason: Three directly relevant sections of one admitted product article corroborate the shared reader, expected job absence and checkpoint limitation. The question's source-platform and coexistence premises match those sections.

optionChallenges.claimRepresented: Restore the stopped replication Log Reader Agent that also supplies CDC capture.
optionChallenges.whyIncorrectInContext: Supported, not incorrect: this SQL Server coexistence configuration intentionally uses one log-reading path for both consumers. Resolving that known stoppage addresses the stated shared dependency while retaining the publication and CDC.
optionChallenges.couldBeCorrectWhen: It is correct in the stated database with a transactional publication and functioning SQL Server Agent. Without a publication, a dedicated CDC capture job is normally relevant instead; a separate downstream consumer fault would require another diagnosis.
optionChallenges.evidenceSummary: Relationship with log reader agent explicitly assigns both consumers to the transactional log reader when replication is present.

optionChallenges.claimRepresented: No dedicated capture job proves that CDC was never enabled.
optionChallenges.whyIncorrectInContext: The stem says CDC previously progressed, and the product article intentionally omits the dedicated capture job when a transactional publication supplies the log reader. Job absence is not proof of CDC being disabled.
optionChallenges.couldBeCorrectWhen: A database never configured for CDC might lack a capture job, but that absence alone is not sufficient evidence even there. In a no-publication design, investigating a missing expected capture job could be useful; the literal proof claim still needs independent configuration evidence.
optionChallenges.evidenceSummary: Agent jobs says the capture job is created only when no transactional publication is defined, whereas the cleanup job is still created.

optionChallenges.claimRepresented: Recreating CDC while retaining replication forces a second independent capture reader.
optionChallenges.whyIncorrectInContext: The source deliberately shares the reader when the publication remains. Disabling/recreating CDC does not supply the promised independent coexistence path and risks changing the consumer's capture configuration instead of correcting the known reader stoppage.
optionChallenges.couldBeCorrectWhen: An intentionally redesigned capture configuration may require enabling or retiring capture instances. The article even supports two overlapping instances for a column-shape transition, but these are not two independent log readers and do not justify C's promise.
optionChallenges.evidenceSummary: The shared-reader section controls coexistence; Handling changes to source table describes overlapping capture instances for schema transition, not separate reader processes.

optionChallenges.claimRepresented: CHECKPOINT removes the need to read outstanding CDC-marked log changes.
optionChallenges.whyIncorrectInContext: The article explicitly states that the truncation point cannot advance past pending marked changes before capture processes them, even in simple recovery. CHECKPOINT neither replaces the stopped log reader nor delivers those changes to CDC.
optionChallenges.couldBeCorrectWhen: Checkpoint is a separate log-management operation after capture requirements and other truncation conditions permit progress. There is no documented context here in which it bypasses pending CDC capture while preserving the consumer contract.
optionChallenges.evidenceSummary: The Important warning in Relationship with log reader agent explicitly rejects truncating pending capture changes by executing CHECKPOINT.

challenges.scope: SQL Server 2022 with a transactional replication publication is specified. Azure SQL Database's separate CDC implementation and unrelated Azure-hosted consumer placement do not change this server-side shared reader.
challenges.plan: Existing successful CDC and replication establish a supported installation. No service-tier upgrade or SQL Server 2025 CES switch is a repair for the documented stopped component.
challenges.role: An administrator must diagnose and resume the relevant agent with appropriate authority. The question does not require a specific SQL permission grant or claim an ordinary application identity may control replication jobs.
challenges.preconditions: SQL Server Agent running, prior capture progress, a retained publication and the observed Log Reader Agent stoppage are explicit. Those premises support the technical key but disclose almost the entire diagnosis.
challenges.featureStatus: This is established CDC/transactional-replication behavior for the stated SQL Server platform, not Preview CES. The current product page distinguishes SQL Server/Managed Instance from Azure SQL Database.
challenges.sourceChanges: I read the actual shared-reader, Agent jobs and CHECKPOINT passages, including capture-instance transitions. The teaching unit's generic CDC statements are not substituted for these precise product rules.
challenges.stemSufficiency: The stem is technically sufficient and arguably too diagnostic: it says capture stops when the named reader stops and asks which action restores their shared dependency.
challenges.explanationBounds: The core explanation is accurate, but its statement about archived questions is an editorial assertion rather than learner-facing technical reasoning. Resume is not guaranteed to fix independent retention, network or consumer failures.
challenges.reasoningDepth: Advanced difficulty is not demonstrated. A learner can select resume the stopped reader without knowing why the dedicated job is absent because the stem already names the shared dependency and alternatives contradict its facts.
challenges.answerClues: B contradicts prior successful CDC; C promises an undocumented extra path; D assumes checkpoint eliminates capture work. A restates the disclosed failure and recovery, leaving no substantial competing diagnosis.

Joining by document fixes the row association but leaves d.Body as the represented text. Whole-document generation could be appropriate for one row per whole document, not this per-chunk contract.

Passing c.chunk correctly represents the stored chunk text. The remaining CROSS JOIN still forms every document/chunk pair, contrary to the original per-source CROSS APPLY relationship. Such a Cartesian product could be intentional for a comparison matrix, not source ownership.

Deduplicating projected rows cannot infer which document owned each chunk, and still invokes the model on d.Body. DISTINCT can remove genuinely repeated identical records after a correct mapping, but it does not repair either semantic defect in this pipeline.

The chunks reference demonstrates per-source CROSS APPLY and embedding c.chunk; the generation reference confirms the source expression determines what is sent. Restoring the DocumentId relationship and using that chunk's text preserves both required invariants. This is static relational/code reasoning, not a claimed SQL execution.

sourceReviews.supportingSummary: The actual SQL Server 2025 reference requires compatibility level at least 170, FIXED chunking and a positive character-count CHUNK_SIZE. It returns chunk and chunk_order and demonstrates per-source CROSS APPLY. Example C inserts each c.chunk together with AI_GENERATE_EMBEDDINGS(c.chunk USE MODEL ...). This directly supports both source correlation and matching the embedded text to the stored chunk. The design training unit explicitly references this function, establishing its immediate parent.

Read the character-source/model arguments, remote enablement/model-access prerequisites, and SELECT/UPDATE plus complete chunk-insertion examples. The full insertion example embeds c.chunk for the corresponding stored chunk. The source has inconsistent return-type prose and one example's c.chunk_text spelling, so the review uses the actual chunk function's returned-column contract and the mutually consistent complete examples, not those errors. No extra API, return-type guarantee or model dimension is invented.

choiceReviews.rationale: Joining on DocumentId restores ownership, but AI_GENERATE_EMBEDDINGS(d.Body ...) still represents the entire document rather than the c.chunk stored in that row. It could be correct for a deliberately whole-document representation, but the candidate explicitly requires one embedding of each row's ChunkText.

Embedding c.chunk fixes the text/vector input, but the retained Cartesian product pairs every chunk with every document ID. It therefore fails per-source ownership. The documented CROSS APPLY pattern retains the source row; merely changing the function argument cannot restore the missing relationship.

DISTINCT does not impose DocumentId equality or change the d.Body argument, so it does not repair either semantic defect. Even considering only row-set semantics, wrong document IDs remain distinct and whole-document embeddings still mismatch stored chunk text. No claim that DISTINCT is supported on vector values is needed or made.

An inner join on d.DocumentId = c.DocumentId retains each document's own CTE chunks, while AI_GENERATE_EMBEDDINGS(c.chunk USE MODEL SupportEmbedding) uses the same text placed in ChunkText. Unique document IDs prevent join fanout, and the declared empty destination avoids an unstated upsert requirement. This reproduces the two relevant invariants of the documented pipeline.

claims.summary: WITH CHECK OPTION keeps rows modified through the view within its selection predicate. It fits writable filtered-view requirements, not preventing an administrator's incompatible base-column DDL.

VIEW_METADATA changes supported clients' browse-mode metadata to describe the view. It can support client cursor scenarios but does not impose the schema dependency restriction needed here.

choiceReviews.rationale: CREATE VIEW's CHECK OPTION paragraph constrains rows modified through the view to its selection criteria. It would address an update that leaves a filtered view, but supplies no dependency binding against the administrator's DROP COLUMN.

The SCHEMABINDING argument explicitly makes ALTER TABLE fail when it affects the view definition. A referenced column is such a dependency. The supplied two-part names satisfy the named-reference requirement, and the administrator is expressly not removing the view or its binding first.

The ENCRYPTION argument concerns stored CREATE VIEW text in sys.syscomments and publication restrictions, not referenced-column DDL. It fits a definition-inspection concern, not the dependency protection asked for; no cryptographic security guarantee is inferred.

VIEW_METADATA changes the browse-mode metadata supplied to DB-Library, ODBC and OLE DB clients. It can describe view columns to updatable cursors, but it does not make the base table schema-bound or reject the stated incompatible ALTER.

claims.summary: Each TVF invocation returns a count row, including zero. The outer WHERE r.ReadyCount > 0 removes exactly zero-count warehouses while retaining their positive aggregate results, so it meets the report contract.
HAVING filters the ungrouped aggregate row itself. A count of zero produces no surviving TVF row, and CROSS APPLY then excludes that warehouse; positive counts remain available to the outer report.

OUTER APPLY is useful when an empty right rowset should still preserve the left row. Here the TVF already returns a zero-valued row, so changing APPLY flavor does not exclude any zero-count warehouse.

COUNT(expression) ignores NULL expressions, but the literal 1 is nonnull for every matching lot. COUNT(1) therefore counts the same matching rows as COUNT(*) and still returns zero in one aggregate row for empty input.

IS NOT NULL can filter a genuinely nullable returned value, but successful COUNT with the stated settings and no overflow returns zero rather than NULL for no matches. It cannot implement positive-count eligibility.

HAVING after the TVF's WHERE filters the ungrouped aggregate row itself. COUNT(*) = 0 fails the positive predicate, so CROSS APPLY receives an empty right rowset and excludes that warehouse. A positive count survives unchanged. SELECT's grammar permits HAVING without a GROUP BY clause.

OUTER APPLY is a left-row preservation mechanism, not a positive-count filter. The present ungrouped TVF already returns a row containing zero, so neither APPLY flavor discards it. OUTER would be useful for the opposite requirement of retaining a parent whose right rowset is empty.

The article limits INLINE to scalar-UDF inlining. OFF can disable that optimization for an applicable scalar function, but does not change a TVF's object kind, introduce a table variable or generate a multistatement implementation.

claims.summary: The unbounded ROWS frame and event ordering compute a global running total, which is useful for a cross-tenant chronology. Without PARTITION BY TenantId, amounts from different tenants enter the same window and violate the independent lifetime totals.

PARTITION BY resets each tenant's calculation, EventTime plus unique EventId resolves ties, and UNBOUNDED PRECEDING through CURRENT ROW includes every earlier tenant event. All three independent requirements are encoded.

RANGE on EventTime includes every timestamp peer together. It can deliberately report a time-bucket cumulative total, but cannot advance separately through tied events in EventId order, which the requested report requires.

The tenant partition and ordering are correct, but one preceding row plus current row forms a two-event moving sum. It fits a rolling comparison, not a lifetime total once a tenant has more than two events.

These rules support separate tenant totals with a complete tie-break order, not whole-SELECT display ordering. SQL Server supports these frame clauses from 2012 onward. The window teaching unit directly references this exact article.

choiceReviews.rationale: Without a tenant partition this is a global cumulative window. An earlier amount for tenant A can enter tenant B's sum. That fits a global chronology, not independent tenant lifetime totals.

TenantId restarts each calculation; EventTime plus per-tenant unique EventId orders peers; the unbounded-preceding ROWS frame includes every earlier tenant event through the current one. All three requirements are encoded while retaining detail rows.

Equal EventTime rows are RANGE peers, so the smaller EventId's frame already includes the larger peer's amount. That fits timestamp-bucket accumulation, not separate advances in the required EventId order.
At a third event, 1 PRECEDING retains only the second and third rows. This is a legitimate two-event rolling sum, not a lifetime total.

claims.summary: decimal(8,4) has p-s = 4 integral digits. It is suitable for values below 10,000 with four decimal places, but cannot represent 99,999.9999 or its negative counterpart.
decimal(9,3) has ample integral capacity but only three fractional digits. It fits a three-decimal measurement contract; rounding a fourth digit violates the required exactness here.
decimal(9,4) allocates five integral and four fractional digits, and precision 9 is in the five-byte tier. It is the smallest precision meeting both exact range and scale requirements.

decimal(10,4) would support a larger integral range, but precision 10 belongs to the nine-byte tier. That extra capacity is useful for a wider domain, not the specified minimum-precision/five-byte design.

sourceReviews.supportingSummary: The actual decimal/numeric reference defines p as digits on both sides of the decimal point and p-s as integral capacity. Its storage table assigns 1-9 precision to five bytes and 10-19 to nine bytes, and its conversion section documents rounding on reduced scale. These exact rules, rather than the parent training unit's incorrect decimal(10,2) five-byte example, determine this question.

choiceReviews.rationale: 8-4 leaves four integral digits, so 99,999.9999 cannot fit. decimal(8,4) would be suitable for a smaller four-integral-digit measurement range while retaining four fractional digits.

Scale 3 loses the fourth fractional digit, for example in 1.2345, even though precision 9 stays in the five-byte tier. It suits a three-fractional-digit domain; that is not the required exact four-place domain.

Five integral digits plus four fractional digits require p=9 and s=4. The sign does not consume a decimal digit, and precision 9 is in the documented five-byte tier. It is the least sufficient precision among these choices.

decimal(10,4) represents the range but uses the documented nine-byte tier and has unnecessary precision. It becomes useful when six integral digits must be represented and the storage requirement allows that larger tier.

claims.summary: SQL Server 2022 supports filtered nonclustered columnstore indexes and the proposed date/decimal columns. The secondary copy preserves the base rowstore and admits only Settled = 1 rows, jointly satisfying all three constraints.

Clustered columnstore can suit an analytics-first table whose base storage may change. It stores the full table rather than a filtered secondary subset, so it violates the required retained rowstore and hot-row exclusion.

An unfiltered nonclustered columnstore is a valid hybrid design when all rows should participate in operational analytics. Here it also maintains unsettled rows in the columnar copy, which the requirements prohibit.

The selected filter is valid, but nvarchar(max) is not a supported nonclustered-columnstore column type. A bounded supported payload type, or a suitable clustered-columnstore design on a platform supporting its LOB branch, is a different context; neither is this unchanged schema.

sourceReviews.supportingSummary: The actual SQL Server CREATE COLUMNSTORE INDEX syntax permits a filtered nonclustered index on selected columns. WHERE is supported for NCCI from SQL Server 2016; date and decimal are supported types, while nvarchar(max) remains excluded from NCCI even where clustered columnstore supports LOBs. The article lists ALTER permission and filtered-index SET options, already supplied by the stem.

The retrieved index unit distinguishes a CCI replacing the base organization from an NCCI that retains the rowstore and provides a separate columnar copy. That distinction supports the base-storage requirement. I did not use its simplified delta-rowgroup threshold or broad performance language to predict a plan or a speedup.

choiceReviews.rationale: NCCI retains the clustered rowstore, uses supported date/decimal columns, and the Settled=1 predicate admits only settled rows. Those three decisions satisfy the combined design contract. If unsettled rows also needed columnar analytics, that filter would instead be inappropriate.

CCI is the base table's columnar organization, not a secondary copy retaining the clustered rowstore, and contains the whole table. It is a legitimate warehouse-first design when rowstore preservation and hot-row exclusion are not requirements.

The selected types and nonclustered placement are valid, but omitting WHERE includes unsettled rows. This would suit whole-table operational analytics if maintaining those rows in the NCCI were acceptable.

The selected nvarchar(max) column makes the NCCI definition unsupported despite the correct filter. The product explicitly restricts LOB support to clustered columnstore in the relevant later releases; alternatively a supported bounded nvarchar column could be in an NCCI if that were the real domain.

claims.summary: The current canonical article explicitly prohibits a primary key on a user-defined history table, even though the current temporal table must have its own primary key. Removing the history key is therefore required; retaining such a key could be appropriate for an ordinary non-temporal archive.

Replacing the history primary key with a UNIQUE index still violates the canonical article's explicit history-table restrictions. A unique index can enforce a key on an ordinary archive table, but is not a supported substitute on the history table being attached here.

The canonical schema-alignment rule requires matching column count, names, order and types. ArchiveBatchId is an extra history-only column, so moving its metadata elsewhere and removing it restores that required alignment without changing the requested temporal record shape.

The current existing-table section allows DATA_CONSISTENCY_CHECK = OFF to skip temporal-data consistency checking when attaching history. It does not permit an extra history column or prohibited key, and the stem already establishes valid nonoverlapping periods.

The current article requires history/current data-type alignment and explicitly calls out matching datetime2 precision. Replacing a history datetime2(7) endpoint with date introduces a mismatch; a date-only field could belong in a separate report but not this unchanged temporal history schema.

The new canonical user-defined-history section bans unique indexes separately from primary keys, so changing only the enforcement object's label does not yield an eligible history table. Its worked history example instead uses nonunique indexes for lookup/analysis. An ordinary independently managed table could need uniqueness, but this system-versioned history role expressly cannot use the proposed UNIQUE substitute.

Even with all original names and types matching, an extra ArchiveBatchId increases the history column count beyond the current table. The canonical alignment rule makes removing that history-only field necessary. Keeping archival batch metadata separately is compatible with the supplied premise; adding such a field to a separate metadata design is different from attaching an unmatched temporal history schema.

The current article allows this switch to skip checking existing current/history period data when versioning is enabled. It does not disable the independent schema-alignment and forbidden-history-key checks. It could be a separate migration choice for an otherwise eligible pair with deliberately handled data validation; here the data is already stipulated valid, while both schema defects remain.

Replacing only the history datetime2(7) endpoints with date makes the two table roles disagree on their period-column type. The canonical article requires aligned types and specifically calls out datetime2 precision alignment. Date-only information may be represented elsewhere for a calendar-oriented use, but cannot replace these matching temporal endpoints while the current table remains unchanged.

claims.summary: An all-JSON document with ISJSON alone is useful for syntax-valid flexible payload storage. It does not supply the separately required typed numeric column or foreign-key column relationship, so it does not meet this relational contract.

Dedicated typed attribute columns can suit a stable predictable schema. Here every newly introduced attribute would require ALTER TABLE, contradicting the requirement to add categories without table DDL.

The training explicitly recommends typed predictable columns plus JSON for variable metadata. This retains ProductId/CategoryId/Price integrity while letting category-specific document shapes evolve without new columns or tables.

Category-specific normalized detail tables are viable when categories and schemas are governed through migrations. The proposed create-a-table-per-category policy violates this application's explicit no-category-driven-DDL requirement.

sourceReviews.supportingSummary: The actual JSON-columns unit explicitly recommends regular typed columns for common product fields and JSON for category-dependent properties without table-structure changes. It also explicitly says earlier SQL Server versions use nvarchar(max). Its unrelated SQL Server 2025 modify-method Preview language is not evidence about the 2022 textual-JSON design here.

The actual overview describes mixing relational columns with JSON text in one table and identifies ISJSON as checking valid JSON. Neither a syntactically valid document nor ISJSON supplies the required numeric Price column or foreign-key relationship. The article's later native-json GA discussion does not backport that type to SQL Server 2022.

The actual foreign-key section defines the engine-enforced column relationship to a referenced table and rejects values absent from that parent key. This directly supports keeping CategoryId in the relational core; arbitrary JSON validity is not such a relationship.

choiceReviews.rationale: A syntactically valid JSON document can omit Price or contain an arbitrary CategoryId; ISJSON does not create the stated typed Price column or referenced-key relationship. Document-only storage is reasonable when those relational invariants are not required, but 'only ISJSON' cannot enforce them here.

Typed core fields satisfy the stable invariants, but adding a column for every newly introduced attribute is table DDL. That model is useful for a stable bounded attribute set where schema changes are permitted, not the stated evolving category contract.

The typed constrained core can enforce an exact nonnull numeric Price and CategoryId foreign key, while nvarchar(max) stores variable JSON shapes without adding category-specific columns or tables. JSON validation may complement that design but is not substituted for relational integrity.

A new detail table is DDL for every category, contradicting the no-category-driven-DDL condition. Category-specific relational tables can be suitable when schemas are stable and stronger per-category typing justifies that maintenance, but not under this requirement.

claims.summary: Allocating 40 then 45 within the first output row assumes one increment per occurrence. The sequence contract instead shares the value for references to the same sequence in one row; separate preceding statements could produce that allocation progression.

Two distinct first-row values are already inconsistent with the same-sequence row rule. Reusing the second value in the next SELECT would also require an unstated restart or different sequence design.

The first row correctly shares 40, but 50 requires another intervening allocation of 45. Such a caller could change the result in a concurrent system, but concurrency and extra statements are explicitly excluded.
The documented same-generator/per-row rule yields (40,40), then the new statement advances the sequence once by five to 45. The no-concurrency and no-restart assumptions make this trace determinate.

sourceReviews.supportingSummary: The actual limitations section says multiple NEXT VALUE FOR occurrences naming the same sequence in one statement return the same value for a given processed row. START WITH and INCREMENT BY control allocation, while separate calls, cached losses and other consumers can create gaps. The two one-row SELECT statements here yield one allocation each.

choiceReviews.rationale: This counts textual NEXT VALUE FOR occurrences as independent allocations within the first row, contrary to the same-sequence-per-row rule. The 40,45,50 progression would fit three separate allocating statements, not these two statements.

The first SELECT cannot produce 40 and 45 from these same-sequence references in one row. Reusing a previously stored 45 in a later projection is a possible application pattern, like the article's allocated local-variable example, but the final statement here requests a new value instead.

The repeated 40s are correct, but 50 requires an additional consumption of 45 between the displayed SELECTs. A concurrent consumer could cause such a gap in another setting; the stem explicitly excludes that and all other additional statements.

One output row in the first SELECT shares allocation 40 across both references. The second SELECT allocates once more and adds the stated increment 5, returning 45. This is row/statement allocation semantics, not a universal gapless-number or uniqueness guarantee.

review.verificationNotes: Statically counted rows and statement boundaries, not function spellings: the first SELECT has one row and the second has one row, so the allocations are 40 then 45. SSMS handles GO; the sequence is new, permissions are supplied and other consumers/restarts are excluded. NO CACHE is valid but is not represented as eliminating every possible production gap. SQL Server 2022 sequence behavior is GA. No SQL was executed. Intermediate is appropriate to the two-step trace; 'this script' unambiguously refers to the displayed code. Direct-003 tests rollback consumption, whereas this new candidate tests same-row reuse. Those related concepts are distinct despite a common source and answer position.
review.confidenceReason: High confidence: the product article states the exact same-sequence/one-row rule and the bounded script provides a deterministic next statement.

optionChallenges.claimRepresented: Each textual occurrence of NEXT VALUE FOR consumes a different value even within one output row.

optionChallenges.couldBeCorrectWhen: Two separate statements could reserve 40 and 45 into variables, then display them together; a later NEXT VALUE FOR would return 50. That is a different allocation statement structure.
optionChallenges.evidenceSummary: The source expressly binds reuse to the same sequence and the same row within a statement; separate requests then follow the defined increment.

optionChallenges.claimRepresented: The first SELECT consumes 40 and 45 from the same generator, yet the next SELECT still returns 45.
optionChallenges.whyIncorrectInContext: The first pair contradicts the same-row sharing rule. It also treats 45 as both already consumed and the next value without any restart or alternate generator in the script.
optionChallenges.couldBeCorrectWhen: With two different sequences, one starting at 40 with increment 5 and another starting at 45, a first SELECT could return (40,45) and a second call to the first generator could return 45. Both references here name the same sequence.
optionChallenges.evidenceSummary: Reuse is expressly limited to instances specifying the same sequence generator; independently defined sequences can have distinct start values and allocation state.

optionChallenges.claimRepresented: Same-row references share 40 but consume enough sequence state for the next statement to return 50.
optionChallenges.whyIncorrectInContext: Sharing 40 for the row does not silently consume 45. The next allocation after the single 40 at increment 5 is 45, not 50.
optionChallenges.couldBeCorrectWhen: Changing the sequence to INCREMENT BY 10 would yield (40,40) then 50; an intervening consumer under increment 5 could also consume 45. Both are excluded by the actual code and assumptions.
optionChallenges.evidenceSummary: The same-row rule fixes one allocation and the sequence definition fixes its increment; the source separately notes shared consumers as a cause of intervening values.

optionChallenges.claimRepresented: One statement-row allocation gives both first-row expressions 40, and the next statement receives 45.
optionChallenges.whyIncorrectInContext: Not incorrect: the first SELECT returns one row and both instances use dbo.PairNumber, satisfying the documented sharing condition. The subsequent statement makes the next allocation under increment 5.
